lines: Control voltages taken from a point travelling round one of four polar equations, drawn on the screen with the point marked in red
Each press moves to the next speed multiplier and the lamp colour shows which — magenta 0.5x, cyan 1x, yellow 2x — though the rate changes by the square of that figure, so 0.5x quarters it
Moves to the previous of the four equations, wrapping from the first round to the last; the equation in force is printed across the top of the screen
Moves to the next of the four equations, wrapping from the last round to the first; the equation in force is printed across the top of the screen
Sets how fast the point travels round the equation; it is ignored entirely while anything is patched to the jack beside it
Sets the first constant of the equation, 0 to 10 in steps of 0.5; the value in force is printed into the equation across the top of the screen
Sets the second constant of the equation, 0 to 10 in steps of 0.5; the value in force is printed into the equation across the top of the screen
Takes over from the speed knob: 0V leaves the point almost stationary, and higher voltages send it backwards round the equation, fastest at 10V
The radius of the point in polar coordinates, ±10V
The horizontal position of the point, its radius times the sine of the angle, ±10V
The vertical position of the point, its radius times the cosine of the angle, ±10V
Note — patching anything into the speed jack cuts the speed knob out altogether; the knob is read only while that jack is empty.
Note — the point never comes to rest: a small fixed amount is added to the angle every sample whatever the speed setting.
Note — the screen is a display and not a control; nothing drawn on it responds to a click or a drag.
Note — there is no reset or sync input, so nothing in the patch can return the point to the start of the equation.

0.why: src/PolarCV.cpp process(): speed_inp = clamp(inputs[SPEED_INPUT].getVoltage(), 0.f, 10.f), read only when isConnected(), one voltage per frame
src/PolarCV.cpp process(): setVoltage(current_cursor.y * 10.0f), where the radius is a sine or cosine and so lies between -1 and 1

1.why: src/PolarCV.cpp process(): setVoltage(carts.x * 10.0f), where carts.x is the radius times sin(theta)

2.why: src/PolarCV.cpp process(): setVoltage(carts.y * 10.0f), where carts.y is the radius times cos(theta)

PolarCV.notes: Three things in this module do not match what it shows or says. First, the speed CV: speed_range_slope is (0.02 - 0.0001) / (0 - 10), which is negative, so 0V gives the slowest forward rate and 10V gives a large negative rate — the CV runs the point backwards and the mapping is plainly the wrong way round. Second, the mult button: the multiplier is applied as cur_mlt * cur_mlt, so the choices printed as 0.5x, 1x and 2x change the rate by 0.25, 1 and 4. Third, the equation printed on the screen for the first of the four reads A sin(theta) + B cos(theta), while the code computes sin(A theta) * cos(B theta); the other three printed forms match their code. Two parameters, CUR_EQ_PARAM and CUR_TIME_MULT_IDX_PARAM, hold the current equation and multiplier as saved state and have no widget on the panel, so they get no line and no tag. The A and B knobs are snapped to whole numbers over 0 to 20 and both displayed and used at half that.
